title: The Feywild House and the Door That Opened Twice: Waluigi’s Cut
subtitle: Gold arguments, fungal gloom, explosives, team branding, and one very disputed entrance
filed: 4 Aethel, 1035 BF — recorded live at the Archive Hall screening desk
kicker: WALUIGI’S CUT · LIVE TRANSCRIPT SCREENING · 1035 BF
pullQuote: “Gold doesn't bring dead people back!” — Wario, while keeping the Contract of Accord in his hand anyway.
standfirst: Waluigi runs the corridor transcript across the Archive Hall projector and stops the scroll every time somebody confuses a contract with a rescue plan. The house appears in fungal light, the party argues about explosives and branding, Beta Luigi arrives at a door that later opens again, and Waluigi supplies the commentary the corridor desperately deserves.

sections.heading: I. “Gold Doesn't Bring Dead People Back!” — Then Why Is the Contract Still in His Hand?
sections.body:
WAH! Start the projector at the corridor argument. Do not skip the first line just because it is already sharp: “Gold? You think I care about gold right now?” The Contract of Accord is held up between them so Mr. T can see it. The parchment cracks in the speaker’s grip. A finger goes into Mr. T’s chest; the voice says this is about getting out before more people end up like Mario, not treasure. Then comes the indictment: “One stupid mistake by ONE person and now we’re all paying for it!” Waluigi pauses the scroll. One person is being blamed, the sentence is already breaking apart, and the speaker still asks for solutions. That is a corridor argument, not a business meeting. WAH!

The Contract flutters in shaking hands. The voice rises, then stalls: “So yes, bring Mario back. Yes, there might be gold in it eventually if you play your cards right.” Arms cross. The speaker hears how pathetic the unfinished thought sounds and does not care today. Mr. T is asked whether he has a better idea. The sentence trails off again. Waluigi taps the projector glass. STOP THERE. NO, freeze that frame. The paper is doing more work than the plan.

Now Wario hits the wall hard enough to leave marks. “Enough!” His voice cracks. He says Mario is gone and asks whether he is supposed to stand here talking like a miracle worker. He waves the Contract and says, “Gold does not bring dead people back.” Waluigi rewinds that sentence twice. It is the cleanest line Wario has had all evening—and the Contract remains in his hand. That is not a charge of fraud. That is Waluigi noticing an object.

Wario starts down the dim corridor without looking back. “Get moving!” Mr. T is coming whether he likes it or not. Wario dismisses his debts, Waluigi’s gambling problems, and the skeletons in Luigi’s closet; fixing this before more people are hurt is what matters. Waluigi stops the image on the Contract thrust toward Mr. T. The search has started moving. The paper is still not explained.

The screening desk can hear the change in the speaker’s voice: accusation, concession, then the request for an answer. Waluigi taps the Contract’s ragged edge on the projected frame. Gold is not the point, the speaker says—unless it eventually is, if Mr. T plays his cards right. That is not a plan. It is a person trying to leave one door open while insisting the room is on fire. Wario’s next sentence hits the wall instead of resolving the argument. Waluigi marks the exact moment the conversation stops being about the reward and becomes about who is going to keep moving.

sections.heading: II. “This Isn't a Book. It's a Contract.” — The Very Helpful Explanation That Never Arrives
sections.body:
Mr. T asks what the document is. Wario stops walking and spins around with the paper clenched so tightly his knuckles go white. “What book?” He holds it up again: the one in his pocket, the one he has been carrying while Mr. T talks about gold. Waluigi circles the worn corners on the screen with a fat purple pointer. Bent. Torn. Handled. Wario says, “This isn't a book. It's a contract.” Splendid. We have identified the genre. We have not identified the terms.

Wario slaps the Contract against his leg. He calls it the only thing keeping him from walking away, because if he does not fix this, “there won't be any coming back—not for anyone.” Then he demands an explanation of Feywild contracts and tells Mr. T to get out of his way if he cannot provide one. Waluigi freezes the frame on the paper again. READ IT. READ THE CONTRACT. If this contract is the hinge of the whole rescue, somebody ought to read the hinge. Nobody does.

Mr. T jokes that Mario is about to have a party. Wario stares at him, jaw working. He rejects the fairy-tale version: no Mario pulled out, no return to normal, no silver lining. “There is only the Feywild. And whatever it did to him.” Waluigi lets that silence stay on screen for a beat. This is the part where Wario admits he is afraid of what happened, and the part where he refuses to make that fear sound pretty. Then he asks if Mr. T has another contract to sell or some magic beans. The paper hits his thigh again.

The group keeps walking through the Feywild. The projector has no distance marker, no hour, and no Feyward clock reading to show. Waluigi does not draw a map in the margin just because the audience wants one. The route comes around a twisted corner; there is the house, and Waluigi is already standing outside it. How he got there ahead of the others? The reel does not show it. WAH! Even Waluigi will not charge the archive for a scene the camera missed.

Wario has to explain the same object twice because Mr. T keeps calling it a book. Waluigi circles the worn corners again. Wario says it is the paper in his pocket, the one he has held for the last five minutes while Mr. T makes small talk about gold. Then he asks, “So either you start explaining what goes on in these Feywild contracts or you can just turn around and get out of my way.” That is the first useful description of the problem: Wario wants the terms, wants the rescue, and has not yet supplied either one.

sections.heading: III. Black Windows, Crooked Hinges, and Waluigi’s Excellent Grimoire Title
sections.body:
Flickering luminescent fungi along the walls bring the house into view. It looks as if it has been cobbled together from the nightmares of a thousand Toads. The windows are black and empty. The door hangs crooked on its hinges; grime coats the surfaces, and vines have started taking the crumbling facade back. The air is still. Waluigi points at the screen: LOOK AT THE WINDOWS. BLACK. EMPTY. Those are not welcoming windows. Those are the eyes of a building that has already decided it dislikes the visitors.

Waluigi asks whether this is the place where Mario is being held. Then he bangs on the door with all his might and shouts, “MARIO! MARIO, IT'S US! WE'RE HERE TO GET YOU OUT!” The old wood creaks under his blows. No voice comes back. Waluigi’s stomach churns at the thought that Mario might be trapped inside, but stomachs are not witnesses and black windows are not a search party. The grimoire comes out. Its yellowed pages turn while Waluigi looks for an entry about the place.

“Feywild Cavern of Despair,” he reads. Waluigi puts a hand to his chest. A magnificent title! A dreadful house! A tremendous mismatch between the confidence of the label and the evidence available. He says Luigi is still outside wailing about Mario, then admits he has not seen Mario himself. The grimoire gives him a phrase, not an address. Waluigi taps the page: do not upgrade a spooky heading into a confirmed location just because it rhymes with the afternoon.

Wario wrinkles his nose at the rot and neglect. “Ugh, this whole place reeks like a Toad's armpit after a week without a shower.” He suggests another way in—or blowing the house to smithereens—and rummages for detonators. Waluigi does not need a second sniff to understand where this is going. The larger charge rises into view. The house has not answered; Wario has brought a question with a FUSE. Waluigi would like the audience to notice the difference.

Waluigi’s first call gets nothing but the creak of the old wood. He leans on the frame, scans the grime and empty windows for a clue, then flourishes the grimoire as if a title might answer for the house. It does not. “Feywild Cavern of Despair” is a good phrase to shout at a locked door; it does not tell Waluigi whether Mario is behind it. The projector pauses on the black windows once more. No movement. No reply. No Mario.

sections.heading: IV. Wario Produces the Detonators; Jory Produces the Consequences
sections.body:
Wario holds up a large, ominous-looking device. Jory Dobbs, walking behind the brothers, asks whether the plan is to blow up the house and hope Mario is inside when it goes wrong. Waluigi points at Jory. There! A sentence with a consequence attached! Jory admits the unknown gives him an adrenaline rush; he also says that does not mean he has to like Wario’s method. The projector catches Wario rummaging for the right charge. Waluigi catches the audience before anyone mistakes rummaging for a safety plan. CHARGE. COAT. NO PLAN.

Waluigi calls the house a prison and a tomb, kicks at the door, and demands a key, a spell, an incantation—“hell, even a rock” if they can be creative. The blows echo in the still air. Wario first refuses to hand over his explosives, saying they cost more than Mr. T’s wardrobe. Then he changes the proposal: Mr. T can throw the charges into the structure while Wario provides a distraction. Wario brings out another wrapped present, crumpled and stained with what looks like old blood. Waluigi pauses the projector. That package is not a party favor. It is also not thrown.

Wario sees what Jory is carrying and reaches toward his shoulder. Jory has a duty ledger under one arm and a reading lamp at his hip, with two more wrapped presents among his things. “Hands off,” Jory snaps. He refuses to toss anything into a structure nobody understands. He says, “Last time I carried someone else's explosives, we crashed a charter plane. Twice.” His thumb finds the dent in his coin purse, the old habit from that crash. Wario is told that if the expedition is paying him, he can handle his own demolition charges.

Waluigi turns to his brother and asks for an explanation. The plan was supposed to be simple: find Mario, extract him from whatever scheme the ghost was part of, and leave. Instead, no one knows where Mario is; Wario is proposing explosives; Luigi is, in Waluigi’s words, somewhere outside being useless. Waluigi’s voice cracks as he says he no longer knows what the point is. The grimoire stays clenched. The house stays shut. WAH! Three facts; zero detonations.

Wario first says the detonators cost more to acquire than Mr. T’s entire wardrobe. Then he keeps them, offers them, takes them back into the plan, and suggests Mr. T do the throwing. Waluigi rewinds that chain. A charge has become a bargaining chip, a distraction, and somebody else’s job, all without going off. The wrapped package in Wario’s coat is crumpled and stained; Jory’s are smaller. Waluigi does not confuse a charge in someone’s hand with a breached house.

sections.heading: V. The Door Opens—and the Figure in It Is Beta Luigi
sections.body:
While the argument continues, the door opens. Everyone turns. Luigi is opening it. Beta Luigi stands just inside the threshold, hands trembling on the frame until his knuckles go white. The smell of mold, rot, and something darker hits him. The floorboards creak under his feet. Waluigi freezes the reel. This is an entrance, yes. It is NOT Mario.

Wario says his name. Beta Luigi calls him “my brother” and says, “I thought... I thought you'd come for me.” His voice catches. He says Wario left them with the ghost and then disappeared. He takes a step and stops. “You're supposed to be in here somewhere.” Waluigi rewinds that line. STOP. REWIND. LISTEN. Who is supposed to be where? The sentence does not say. Waluigi does not get to solve the pronoun by wishing harder, and the dark space behind Beta Luigi remains unseen.

Waluigi slams his grimoire onto a nearby rock. “ENOUGH!” He tells Luigi he cannot wander out of a scheme and expect everyone else to fix it. He turns on Wario: they came for a plan and still do not know where Mario is. Then he turns on Mr. T, calling him Wario’s personal luggage rack and telling him to get out before the explosives start. The pen clicks in Waluigi’s hand; his grip tightens.

Beta Luigi asks Waluigi to stop saying his name like that. The explanation comes in fragments. Mario was supposed to be counting on him. When Mario was gone and the ghost appeared, Beta Luigi did not have the courage to try to save him. The film shows a trembling hand on the frame and a person who has not stepped farther into the room. It does not show Mario. Waluigi lowers the projector speed. That distinction is the whole scene.

Beta Luigi’s voice cracks as he says he thought Wario would come for him. He says Wario left them with the ghost, then adds that someone is supposed to be inside. Waluigi stops on that pronoun again. The line does not identify Mario as the person behind the door. The doorway scene has its own claim of abandonment and its own fear; it does not turn either into a sighting of the missing brother.

sections.heading: VI. “I Want to Rescue Mario”—Not the Same as “I'm Brave”
sections.body:
Mr. T asks Beta Luigi whether courage has returned. Beta Luigi repeats the word as if it belongs in a dusty manual and asks what courage matters anymore. A grimoire slams shut hard enough to make everyone wince. The voice is identified as Wario’s; Waluigi pauses the frame because a grimoire had been in Waluigi’s hands moments earlier. WHO HAS THE BOOK? THE TAPE DOES NOT SAY. The recording does not explain the handoff. Waluigi will not invent one just to keep the props tidy.

Wario steps close and tells Beta Luigi they will get back to the Contract and find Mario. They will not do it by “standing around crying about our feelings in the middle of some creepy Feywild shithole.” Every minute spent arguing, Wario says, is another minute Mario could be somewhere worse. He jabs a finger into Beta Luigi’s chest. Beta Luigi flinches and says, “Stop it.” He closes his eyes, tries to breathe, opens them, then loses the sentence he was trying to say. He did not know if he would come back at all; every step toward the house felt like moving backward through what went wrong.

Then comes the answer. Beta Luigi says he wants to rescue Mario, but insists that this does not make him brave. Waluigi drops the performance for three sentences. No shouting. No bit. Just the scene. Beta Luigi is frightened. He says so plainly. Wanting to help does not erase the fear, and Wario has not talked him out of it. That is an honest answer. Waluigi holds the frame there—then snaps back: Wario takes the yes, grins, pokes Beta Luigi in the chest, and says they leave in five minutes whether he is ready or not.

“Luigi, you coming?” Wario calls over his shoulder, asking if they should drag him back to civilization. Something is coming out of Wario’s coat, but the recording never identifies it. Waluigi zooms in anyway. The hand is moving; the five-minute clock is not.

Wario’s first demand is not gentle. He says every wasted minute is a minute Mario could be somewhere worse, then presses the question again while Beta Luigi stands frozen and looks toward the grimoire. Beta Luigi closes his eyes and tries to breathe. Waluigi watches the pause without calling it weakness. The answer comes only after the struggle to say it. The five-minute deadline arrives afterward, as Wario turns away and pulls at his coat. He has a yes. He does not have a proof of courage, and he does not have Mario.

sections.heading: VII. A Rescue Party Spends Its Time Naming Itself
sections.body:
Waluigi snatches the grimoire back from Wario and warns him not to set off the blasting caps. NO BLAST. NO RUBBLE. NO HEROIC ENTRANCE. A structure this unstable could bring the masonry down on the group. Waluigi proposes a concentrated arcane ray; Jory is told to hold the perimeter. Then Mr. T asks whether they should form a party before going in and opens the form screen on a Walupedia tablet marked “PROTOTYPE — PROPERTY OF WARIO.” Waluigi pauses. The door is still locked. The branding meeting has begun.

Wario grabs the tablet. Wario says he does not do parties; he does enterprises. He dismisses “The Brave Ones” as too much effort and “The Sad Brothers” as a branding nightmare, then proposes “Wario's Relentless Recovery Unit.” Waluigi calls it a janitorial service. Mr. T suggests “Superstars.” Waluigi protests that he is the only superstar in the damp corridor. He wants “The Waluigi Vanguard,” because he is holding the magic while Wario holds the explosives. Waluigi points at the tablet as though a correct name could force it to respect him.

Jory calls “Waluigi Vanguard” a private security firm for a moody aristocrat. He invokes the 1032 BF expedition-branding guidelines, warns about a name that might invite a tax-evasion inquiry at the border, and proposes “The Loot-Lifters” or “The Debt-Collectors.” Wario rejects “lift,” denies having debts, calls them “outstanding investments,” and declares “Wario's Golden Heist!” He slams the tablet onto a crate. The screen flickers.

Beta Luigi shrinks back. Beta Luigi says the name is only a label on a box. He says the walls are breathing and asks them to let Waluigi do the magic before all this talk invites something to listen. Jory offers to type “The Loot-Lifters” for now; a better idea, he jokes, costs a three-coin consultation fee. Wario shakes the tablet and threatens to dock Jory’s nonexistent shares for every second spent thinking about aesthetics. Waluigi stares at the blinking screen. BRAND. TABLET. CRATE. FLICKER. A declared name is not a submitted name, and neither one opens the door. WAH!

sections.heading: VIII. The Coin, the Ice, and the Door That Somehow Opens Again
sections.body:
Mr. T walks to the door with a coin and starts picking the lock. Waluigi hisses at Mr. T to move aside. He shoves past and snatches the coin before it reaches the keyhole. Waluigi boasts about the precision of his ice magic. Waluigi presses his palm to the wood and sends a thin, freezing stream of mana toward the lock. He demands silence. Nobody is to let Wario sneeze on the workspace. Waluigi stops the tape on the frost-blue light at his fingertips. FREEZE FRAME. LOOK AT THE HANDS. THIS is the part where the magic is actually being done.

A jagged crack splits the frame. Waluigi pulls back and says the door frame is failing. He scribbles an accusation of sabotage by incompetence on his working papers, blaming Mr. T’s lack of finesse, then stomps the floorboards and drives ice-magic into the ground. Now he says he is reinforcing the hinge so the door will fall away from them. Wario argues that a little damage is a discount on the entry fee. Wario objects that he does not blow things up; he secures assets. He says the blast would bury the gold beneath rubble; he is an accountant, he follows the path of least resistance to maximum profit. Waluigi points out that Wario could be flattened before he reaches the room—and the blast could shatter the grimoire.

Waluigi tells Wario to stop shouting. He says the lock is held in place and gives the group exactly sixty seconds to move while he maintains the ice-seal. If they do not move, he will release the freeze and let the door settle into its ruin. Jory is ordered to watch the perimeter; the rest are told to follow Waluigi in single file. Waluigi’s breath comes in thin wisps. His hands tremble under the effort. Wario keeps arguing about being first; Waluigi warns that one wrong tremor could leave them staring at a wall of debris.

Mr. T asks whether Waluigi opens the door. The frost pulses in controlled bursts; Waluigi tests the door with careful pressure. Waluigi snaps that he is not concerned about being watched. Then comes the click. Waluigi smiles, steps back from the frozen seal, and says, “The door yields to precision and patience.” He has opened it. Except the tape already showed Beta Luigi opening it earlier. Waluigi looks directly at the projector. CLICK. OPEN. STOP. No, the film does not tell us why the same door needs opening twice. Waluigi will not splice in a missing scene. The cut ends at the threshold: NO ENTRY, no search, no Mario.
